claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has a single-phase FCC matrix.
The as-manufactured alloy has minimal preexisting oxide films.
Oxidizing and reducing gas environments will be compared while elevated-temperature exposure conditions are otherwise controlled.
The proposed exposure range is approximately 600–800 °C for times sufficient to produce measurable oxidation.
Oxidizing gases cause preferential Ti and Cr oxidation along grain boundaries in this alloy.
Preferential grain-boundary oxidation produces a porous, non-protective oxide scale.
The porous oxide scale induces internal stresses.
Grain-boundary oxide formation weakens intergranular cohesion and causes local embrittlement and crack initiation.
Oxidation-induced loss of intergranular cohesion facilitates rapid crack propagation and can cause catastrophic failure.
Reducing atmospheres suppress oxidation-induced damage relative to oxygen-rich atmospheres.
Oxidizing exposure will produce more pronounced grain-boundary oxidation than reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce intergranular fracture toughness relative to reducing exposure.
Catastrophic failure will begin earlier after oxidizing exposure than after reducing exposure.
Samples exposed to reducing conditions will retain better mechanical integrity and show minimal grain-boundary oxidation.
The proposed oxidation-controlled behavior applies within approximately 600–800 °C after sufficiently long exposure.
Minor alloying elements and processing-induced microstructural variations may modulate oxidation behavior.
The mechanism would be falsified if oxidizing and reducing exposures produce no significant difference in grain-boundary oxidation and mechanical degradation.
The mechanism would also be falsified if catastrophic failure does not preferentially correlate with grain-boundary oxidation.
